clinical_knowledge.topic: Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Admit to Neuro-ICU, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: thunderclap headache described as worst headache of life accompanied by neck stiffness and photophobia

Key HPI features: 52F suddenly experienced an explosive, excruciating 'thunderclap' headache while straining during bowel movement 3 hours ago. Describes it as 'being struck in the back of the head with a baseball bat' and rates pain 10/10. Accompanied by two episodes of projectile vomiting, severe photophobia, nuchal rigidity, and transient confusion.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: HR 94, BP 185/104, Temp 37.1C. GCS 14 (E3 V5 M6 - lethargic but oriented). Marked nuchal rigidity with positive Kernig and Brudzinski signs. Cranial nerves intact. Non-contrast head CT reveals hyperdense blood filling the basal cisterns, Circle of Willis, and bilateral Sylvian fissures (Modified Fisher Grade 3). CT angiography (CTA) of head confirms a 7 mm anterior communicating artery (ACom) saccular aneurysm with irregular bleb.
Relevant background/PMH: Hypertension, 30 pack-year smoking history
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Thunderclap migraine without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Confusion or declining consciousness — signals a more severe bleed or rebleeding risk.
management_principles: Maintain strict blood pressure control (Systolic BP < 140 mmHg) using continuous IV Nicardipine or Labetalol infusion until aneurysm securing
Start oral Nimodipine 60 mg q4h for 21 days to prevent delayed cerebral vasospasm
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 52F presenting with abrupt-onset thunderclap headache, meningismus, and photophobia classic for aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: HR 94, BP 185/104, Temp 37.1C. GCS 14 (E3 V5 M6 - lethargic but oriented). Marked nuchal rigidity with positive Kernig and Brudzinski signs. Cranial nerves intact. Non-contrast head CT reveals hyperdense blood filling the basal cisterns, Circle of Willis, and bilateral Sylvian fissures (Modified Fisher Grade 3). CT angiography (CTA) of head confirms a 7 mm anterior communicating artery (ACom) saccular aneurysm with irregular bleb.
reference_soap.assessment: Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (aSAH) secondary to ruptured Anterior Communicating Artery (ACom) aneurysm (Hunt and Hess Grade II).
reference_soap.plan: Admit to Neuro-ICU. Maintain strict blood pressure control (Systolic BP < 140 mmHg) using continuous IV Nicardipine or Labetalol infusion until aneurysm securing. Start oral Nimodipine 60 mg q4h for 21 days to prevent delayed cerebral vasospasm. Consult neurosurgery and interventional neuroradiology for urgent endovascular coiling vs surgical clipping within 24 hours. Place external ventricular drain (EVD) if acute hydrocephalus develops.

learning_objectives: Identify clinical hallmarks of aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (thunderclap headache, meningeal irritation signs)
Interpret CT findings of subarachnoid blood and understand indications for lumbar puncture (xanthochromia) if CT is negative
Explain the critical rationale and dosing schedule for enteral Nimodipine in preventing delayed cerebral vasospasm
Compare endovascular coiling vs microsurgical clipping strategies for securing intracranial aneurysms

teaching.one_liner: A ruptured brain aneurysm bleeds into the space around the brain, causing an instantaneous 'thunderclap' headache often triggered by straining — a neurosurgical emergency needing the aneurysm secured (coiling or clipping) within 24 hours.
red_flags: Confusion or declining consciousness — signals a more severe bleed or rebleeding risk

must_ask.say: What were you doing when the headache started, and how quickly did it become unbearable?
Is this the worst headache of your life?
Any vomiting, neck stiffness, or sensitivity to light?
Did anyone in your family have a brain aneurysm or die of a brain bleed?
Do you smoke, and how is your blood pressure controlled?

history.answer: Doctor, I have the worst headache of my entire life. It hit me all of a sudden like a bomb going off in my head.
It happened completely out of nowhere three hours ago, reaching maximum 10 out of 10 pain within just a couple of seconds.
This is the first time I have ever had a headache this severe. I get mild tension headaches once in a while, but nothing even remotely like this.
It started right at the back of my head and neck, but now my entire head is throbbing horribly.
It felt like being struck in the back of the head with a baseball bat. The pain is an excruciating 10 out of 10 explosive pressure.
It has been severe and continuous without any relief for the past three hours since it started.
Any slight movement of my head or neck makes the agony much worse, and lying down does not help at all.
No, there were no flashing lights, blind spots, numbness, or warnings before it hit.
Yes, I had two episodes of projectile vomiting, and the lights in this room make my head hurt terribly. Loud sounds bother me as well.
No, I have not had any runny nose, tearing, red eye, or drooping eyelid.
My neck is terribly stiff and painful to bend forward, but I have not noticed chills or any skin rash.
I felt a bit confused and dazed right after it struck, but I have not had any weakness, numbness, slurred speech, or seizures.
No, my vision is not blurred or doubled, and my eyes do not hurt inside.
No, my temples are not tender to the touch, and I do not have jaw pain when chewing or body aches.
No, I did not hit my head or have any fall or accident.
I took two acetaminophen tablets right after it started, but they did not touch the pain at all. I rarely take painkillers otherwise.
It struck right when I was straining hard during a bowel movement on the toilet.
No one else around me has a headache, and we do not use any gas or fuel-burning heaters at home.
No, I have never had cancer, HIV, or any condition affecting my immune system.
I am terrified that an artery burst inside my brain and is bleeding right now.
I am terrified I am going to die or suffer a major stroke just like my mother did.
I need a brain CT scan immediately and emergency surgery to seal off whatever is bleeding in my head.
I was diagnosed with high blood pressure five years ago, but I do not have any other medical conditions.
I had a normal gallbladder removal about ten years ago and have never stayed in the hospital otherwise.
I am prescribed lisinopril 20 milligrams once a day for high blood pressure, but to be honest, I often forget to take it.
No, I do not have any allergies to medications or anything else.
I have smoked one pack of cigarettes every day for the past 30 years, and I still smoke.
I have a glass of wine on occasional weekends, but nothing more than that.
I work as a retail department supervisor and live with my husband.
My mother died suddenly in her fifties from a ruptured brain aneurysm, which is why I am so frightened.
My last menstrual period was about three years ago; I went through natural menopause, and there is no chance of pregnancy.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 185/104 mmHg, heart rate 94 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, temperature 37.1°C, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Lethargic and groaning from severe pain, but oriented to person, place, and time with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 14.
Marked resistance to passive neck flexion with positive Kernig and Brudzinski signs.
Pupils are equal, round, and reactive to light; funduscopic exam shows sharp optic disc margins without papilledema, and extraocular movements are intact.
Cranial nerves II through XII are grossly intact without facial asymmetry, ptosis, or tongue deviation.
Normal 5/5 muscle strength throughout all four extremities with symmetric tone.
Intact light touch and pinprick sensation symmetrically across all dermatomes.
Symmetric 2+ deep tendon reflexes at biceps, patella, and Achilles bilaterally; plantar responses are flexor.
No tenderness to palpation over bilateral temporal arteries, frontal and maxillary sinuses, or paracervical muscles.
